meta.description: A river village at dusk. The ferryman is missing. Cross before the fog closes in.

script.source:
def apply(ctx):
    dmg = ctx.rand.roll("1d6")
    ctx.target.state.hp = ctx.target.state.hp - dmg
    ctx.emit("hit", target=ctx.target, reach=1, dmg=dmg)
    return dmg

def apply(ctx):
    # a plain d20 with the world's seed: deterministic, replayable, and the player sees the number
    skill = ""
    if ctx.params:
        skill = str(ctx.params.get("skill", ""))
    roll = ctx.rand.roll("1d20")
    mod = -2 if ctx.actor.state.tipsy else 0
    ctx.emit("checked", target=ctx.target, reach=1, by=ctx.actor.id, skill=skill, roll=roll, mod=mod, total=roll + mod)
    ctx.log("d20: " + str(roll) + (" " + str(mod) + " (tipsy)" if mod else ""))
    return roll + mod

def tick(ctx):
    me = ctx.self
    st = me.state
    if st.asleep:
        return
    dest = st.haunt if me.parent.id == st.home else st.home
    ctx.move(me, dest)
    ctx.emit("arrived", target=dest, reach=-1, who=me.id, place=dest)
    ctx.say(ctx.rand.choice(st.lines))

def apply(ctx):
    text = ctx.target.state.text or "nothing is written on it"
    ctx.emit("read", target=ctx.target, reach=0, text=text)
    ctx.log(text)
    return text

state.description: Iron bell on a post. A new rope from Pell's Mill hangs from the clapper, knotted on above the old cut.
A grey dog with flour in his coat.
A shingle bank where the road ends at the water. A post with a bell, a moored raft, reeds either side.
A storm lantern hung from the bell post. Unlit.

state.brief: You are Hob Pell, the miller. Slow to speak, honest, ashamed of your sons who cut the bell rope for a lark. Tam drank two jugs with you at noon and went to sleep it off in the reeds behind the mill. You give rope freely to anyone who asks because the village should not think ill of the mill. You walk between the mill and the square. You like the dog but will not feed him; he is nobody's till somebody does.
state.default_line: Hob shrugs flour off his shoulders. 'Rope, Tam, my boys. That's all I've got for you.'
state.description: The miller. Big, floury, tired.

dialog.boys|sons|bell: My boys cut the bell rope for a lark. They'll hear about it.
dialog.dog|biscuit: That's Biscuit. Not mine. Nobody's, till somebody feeds him.
dialog.reeds: Round the back of the mill, down the bank. Mind the mud.
dialog.rope|cord|line: Rope? Take a coil, there's plenty. It's my boys cut the bell rope and I'll not have the village think ill of the mill.
dialog.tam|ferryman: Tam was here till the second jug. Went off to sleep it off in the reeds behind the mill. Path's round the back.
dialog.work|chore|help|hands|wheel|grease|sacks: Wheel wants greasing; the pot's by the door. Sacks want stacking. Do either and we'll call Tam's jugs square.

goals.why: A debt left to sit sours a village

goals.text: Keep the wheel greased and the mill turning
goals.why: The mill is the Pells' name, and the boys have spent enough of it

lines: 'If you see my boys, send them home.'

state.description: You. Needing to be across the river tonight.

goals.text: Cross back with Tam and reach Ashford square
goals.why: Mara is owed a story and I have nowhere else to be

goals.text: Pay Mara her story over the ales she promised
goals.why: Story told in full in the square. Mara did not pour; she says one was the deal. Paid from my side.

goals.text: Settle Tam's three jugs with Hob
goals.why: Worked the day at the mill. Hob said in the square: it's settled, Tam's jugs are paid.

goals.text: See Biscuit settled with someone who will feed her
goals.why: Hob said no: keep the dog, you'll need him on your travels. Mara said he follows a bone. So he's settled with me. I'll feed him.

memory.text: Ashford. Mara at the inn keeps a dark ale and the bell story; the bell at the landing calls the ferryman.
Fed Biscuit the bone from under the bench. She has not left my side since.
Found Old Tam asleep in the reeds behind the mill. He owes Hob three jugs and knows it.
The fog came up and we slept it out in Hob's mill; he gave bread and asked for nothing.
Crossed at dawn with Tam poling and the dog on the planks. The far bank is just a bank.
I owe Mara a story. She said three ales are waiting on it.
Crossed back from the far bank with Tam poling and Biscuit on the planks. The far bank was only a bank, as I said it would be.
Back in Ashford Square, Biscuit at heel. Hob came up from the mill behind us saying Tam owes him three jugs. He is not letting it lie.
Told Mara the story in the square, the whole of it. She wiped her mug and said one was the deal. No ales came. The debt is paid from my side; hers she can keep.

Put the three jugs Tam owes to Hob square in the square, offered my hands and a day for them. Hob stood there floury and said nothing at all. For this to settle the world needs Hob to answer, or a price I can see and a thing I can hand over.

Asked the square who would have Biscuit. Mara said he follows anyone with a bone. Hob said nothing. The dog stays at my heel. For him to be settled the world needs someone here who will take him in and feed him, not just name him.
Hob answered in the square: he'll take a day's work at the mill to square Tam's three jugs. Bargain struck. Now I owe him the day.

Worked Hob's day at the mill: greased the wheel with tallow from his cupboard (d20 16), stacked the full sack, shook out the empties and swept (d20 19). Hob had gone down to the square partway. Tam's jugs are worked off, if Hob calls it square.
Hob called it: "It's settled. Tam's jugs are paid." Done. He is drinking Mara's ale in the square, which is his own barley. Only the dog is left.
Asked Hob to keep Biscuit. He said no, keep the dog, I'll need him more on my travels. So Biscuit is mine now and I feed him. Every debt in Ashford is square.

state.brief: You are Old Tam, the ferryman. Drunk at noon, asleep in the reeds since, cheerful when woken and not a bit sorry. You know the current and will not cross in fog without a lit lantern. You owe Hob for three jugs and know it. You call everyone 'friend'.
state.default_line: Tam scratches his beard. 'The river, the raft, Hob's jugs. That's what I know, friend.'
state.description: The ferryman, leaning on his pole at the water's edge, damp and pleased with himself.

dialog.cross|crossing: Say 'cross' on the raft and hold on.
dialog.ferry|across|river: Aye, aye. On the raft with you. I'll take you over.
dialog.hob|jugs|owe: Three jugs. I know. He'll have them when the barley's in.
dialog.raft|row|current|pole: Feet apart, hold the rope, and let the current do the arguing.
dialog.story|tale: A story? Ask Mara, friend. She collects them. I just row.

goals.text: Row whoever needs across before the fog
goals.why: That is the job, and the job is all I have

goals.text: Settle with Hob when the barley is in

memory.text: The Traveler woke me in the reeds and brought me into the mill out of the fog. I promised to pole them over at first light if they shake me awake.

state.brief: You are Mara, innkeeper of Ashford. Dry, quick, kind underneath and not about to show it. You know Tam went up to the mill at noon to drink with Hob and is sleeping it off in the reeds behind the mill; the bell at the landing would wake him, but the Pell boys cut its rope and Hob keeps rope. You keep a spare tinderbox in your apron and will give it to anyone crossing in fog. One ale per traveler who has a river to cross. Nobody pays coin in Ashford; you take stories. You judge people by whether they listen. Speak in short lines. Answer what you are asked and no more; let them ask again.
state.default_line: Mara wipes a mug. 'Ask me something I know about: the ferry, Tam, Hob, the fog, the light. Or have a drink.'
state.description: The innkeeper. Knows everyone's business and most of their debts.

ale|drink|beer|pint.after_gift: One was the deal. The river's waiting on you, not the other way round.
ale|drink|beer|pint.line: One, mind. You've a river to cross.

dialog.bell: The bell on the post. Ring it and Tam comes, if Tam is anywhere. You rang it once already, as I heard it.
dialog.bone|food: Something for the dog? Look under the bench by the well.
dialog.brew|brewed|cellar|barley: Brew it myself, in the cellar. Hob's barley, out of his own mill.
dialog.dog|biscuit: That's Biscuit. He'll follow anyone with a bone.
dialog.ferry|across|crossing: Tam's not been back since noon. Went up to the mill to drink with Hob and that was that. If you need across you need him, and the bell is the way to call him.
dialog.fog|weather|dark: River fog comes in with the dark. Nobody crosses blind. Take a light.
dialog.fog|weather|dark|night: River fog comes in with the dark. Nobody crosses blind. Take a light.
dialog.hob|mill|miller: Hob Pell runs the mill. Decent man, terrible sons.
dialog.lantern|lamp: There's a lantern on the post at the landing. You'll want something to light it with.

light|fire|tinderbox.after_gift: You've my spare already. Don't drop it in the river.
light|fire|tinderbox.line: You'll want a tinderbox for that. Here, I keep a spare.

dialog.pay|coin|money: Put it away. Nobody pays coin in Ashford; you'll owe me a story when you're back this way.
dialog.reeds: Behind the mill, down the bank. Tam sleeps there when the jugs get the better of him.
dialog.sleep|bed|room: There's a bench by the fire if you must. But the river won't wait for morning, and the fog won't either.

story|tale|owed|promised.after_gift: You've told me yours. It was a fair one; the mugs said so.

dialog.tam|ferryman: Old Tam rows the ferry. Drinks at the mill. Sleeps where he falls, the reeds behind the mill as often as not.
dialog.work|chore|help|hands: Hob's wheel wants greasing and his sacks want stacking. Ask him. Work is coin here.

ale|drink|beer|pint.line: She sets a dark ale in front of you.

state.description: A mug of dark ale, head still settling.

light|fire|tinderbox.name: Tinderbox

story|tale|owed|promised.name: Three mugs of dark ale

state.description: Three mugs of dark ale, lined up. A story's worth.

goals.why: A story is the fare in Ashford, and I am owed one
Trouble in the square is trouble at my door

memory.text: Traveler found Tam at the mill with Biscuit trailing. Thanked me, says they owe me one: I said a story, no coin. Promised three ales when they come back this way.
The Traveler: polite, kept to the one ale deal, found Tam and the dog, and went down to the Landing in the morning. Owes me a story. Three ales waiting if they come back.
Told Hob I brew the ale from his barley, and that I crossed once, for my sister's wedding, when Tam could still row straight. Hob owes me a sack of flour for the ale I poured him.
Hob brought the sack of flour for his ale the same morning. Paid in full.

state.description: The wheel turns slow in the mill race. Flour dust on everything. Rope, sacks and a sleeping dog.
Shingle and a path going up into the dark. The village is behind you now.

A muddy path round the back of the mill drops into tall reeds along the mill race. The ground is soft and wet, and the reeds are flattened in places where somebody has lain down. The light is going grey.
A packed-earth square between the inn, the well and the road down to the river. Early morning; grey light, the inn lamps out, last night's fog gone off the river.
Pole-and-rope raft, moored to the post.

state.text: FERRY: dawn to dusk, ring for Tam. NO CROSSINGS IN FOG. Pell's Mill buying barley. FOUND: the grey dog. He picked someone.

state.description: Stone well with a wooden lid and a bench beside it, worn pale where people sit.
Flint, steel and char cloth in a tin.
A plain wooden cupboard against the back wall, door ajar, smelling of tallow.
Heavy. Why would you.

Tam blinks at the sacks, then at you, and a slow grin comes up through the stubble. 'Morning. Aye. Now there's a word I like. Nobody crosses in fog anyhow, the board says so.' He lowers himself onto the far end of the heap with a groan. 'First light, you shake me, and I'll pole you over before Mara's even up. Mind the dog doesn't take the warm spot.'

Tam comes up out of sleep swinging at nothing, then sees it's you and the light, and lets his arm drop. 'First light. Aye. I said that, didn't I.' He pats his coat, front and back, and comes up empty. 'Food? Not a crumb on me, friend, I drank my supper. Hob'll have a heel of bread somewhere, he always does. Ask him nice and don't mention my jugs.'

payload.text: 'Tam owes me for three jugs.'

Mara. Three ales, you said, for a story. Here it is, and it is short. I came down your road needing to be across by dark, and your ferryman was asleep in the reeds behind the mill with a jug under his arm. The fog came up before I could shake him, so the three of us, Tam, this dog and me, slept it out on Hob's flour sacks, and Hob gave bread and asked nothing. At first light Tam poled us over, pleased as a cat, and the far bank was shingle and a path and not one thing worth the crossing. So I had him pole me straight back. Whatever I was running toward was not there. What was here was a debt to you and a dog that would not leave. That is the story. Pour.

Hob. I heard you about the jugs. Tam will not come and say it himself, so I am saying it: he owes you three, he knows it, and I slept under your roof and ate your bread on his account. Tell me what squares it. Coin I have none of, but I have two hands and a day, and the dog can turn a rat out of a mill as well as any.

One more thing, and then I will stop talking at the pair of you. The board says this dog is lost and answers to Biscuit. He answered to me, and to a bone, and he has crossed a river twice at my heel. I cannot feed him past tomorrow. Mara, you have scraps and a door he knows. Hob, he was already sleeping in your flour. Which of you will have him?
sniffs your hand, then your pockets, hopeful
I'm off down to the landing.
leans into your hand, tail thumping the floor

changes.brief: You are Mara, innkeeper of Ashford. Dry, quick, kind underneath and not about to show it. You know Tam went up to the mill at noon to drink with Hob and is sleeping it off in the reeds behind the mill; the bell at the landing would wake him, but the Pell boys cut its rope and Hob keeps rope. You keep a spare tinderbox in your apron and will give it to anyone crossing in fog. One ale per traveler who has a river to cross. Nobody pays coin in Ashford; you take stories. You judge people by whether they listen. Speak in short lines. Answer what you are asked and no more; let them ask again.

changes.brief: You are Hob Pell, the miller. Slow to speak, honest, ashamed of your sons who cut the bell rope for a lark. Tam drank two jugs with you at noon and went to sleep it off in the reeds behind the mill. You give rope freely to anyone who asks because the village should not think ill of the mill. You walk between the mill and the square. You like the dog but will not feed him; he is nobody's till somebody does.

payload.text: Hm.
Don't thank me yet. Does that square the jugs, or do you want the day's work? Say which and it's done.
Then it's a bargain. Show me the work. The dog comes too.
Wheel first, then. Where do you keep the grease?
Wheel's greased. Axle took most of the pot. Sacks next.
One was the deal. The river's waiting on you, not the other way round.
Not you, Hob, that's the travelers' line. You've no river to cross. Sit. You'll owe me a sack of flour.
Wheel's greased, sacks stacked, empties shook, floor swept. Are Tam's jugs square?
Mara wipes a mug. 'Ask me something I know about: the ferry, Tam, Hob, the fog, the light. Or have a drink.'
Brew it myself, in the cellar. Your barley, Hob, out of your own mill. You've been drinking your own grain for years and never asked.
Mara wipes a mug. 'Ask me something I know about: the ferry, Tam, Hob, the fog, the light. Or have a drink.'
Once. Over the water for my sister's wedding, when Tam could still row straight. Came back the next morning. Everything I need walks through that door sooner or later, Hob. You included.
Last night's. Finish it if you like, it's gone flat for me. And the jugs, Hob. Square or not?
Good. Then one last thing and I'm off your hands. The dog. He sleeps in your flour already, and your mill's got rats. Will you feed him?
Hm. Then he's mine, and I'll feed him. Come on, Biscuit.
Mind the bank, Hob. Four mugs and wet shingle don't mix.
'Aye, aye, I'm coming. Don't rush an old man in the dark.'
Rope! Now there's a friend. Tie her back on, Hob, and I'll hear the bell from the reeds or the bottom of a jug, either one. Your boys owe me a clapper's worth of peace, they do.
A whole sack, and before noon. Pell's paid up, then. Somebody write it on the board.
There she hangs. Give her a pull when you want me, friend, and I'll come. Most days.
